div.head: Multivariate Adaptive Regression Spline (MARS) is a simple
div.p: and powerful non-parametric machine learning algorithm that automatizes the selection of non-linear terms in regression models. In this study, we propose using MARS in a spatial regression framework to account for potential nonlinearities and spatial effects in spatial regression models.

Using a relatively large data set of 17,000 dwellings in St. Petersburg (Russia), we examine how this algorithm works. The empirical evidence shows that most explanatory variables in the spatial regression model-including the spatial lag of the dependent variable-have a non-linear impact on the asking prices of dwellings.

The recent contribution of Kopczewska (2022) provides an overview of the existing spatial toolbox proposed in the literature for supervised and unsupervised learning, which displaces classical spatial econometrics. Some of the most popular machine learning methods were adapted to include the spatial component with the objective of incorporating spatial references in the analysis. For example, a modification of the regression trees algorithm to identify convergence clubs using filtered spatial regression models is proposed by Postiglione et al. (2010). Paez et al. (2019) include the coordinates of observations and interactions to improve the classification algorithm of regression trees. Sommervoll and Sommervoll (2019) use machine learning methods in the form of genetic algorithms to aggregate spatial units and show that they outperform conventional econometric models with fixed spatial effects. Dong et al. (2015) demonstrate that support vector machine (SVM) models accounting for spatial proximity outperform non-spatial models in terms of model fitting and predictive performance. Andris et al. (2013) use SVM to investigate geographic patterns. Sinha et al. (2019) show that the random forest model is sensitive to spatial autocorrelation, which leads to an increase in the variance of the residuals. Finally, Cajias and Ertl (2018) test explanatory power by means of outof-sample validation approaches using the generalized additive model (GAM) for spatial hedonic modeling. In general, this research shows how regional science and urban economics can benefit from the use of machine learning techniques.

In this paper, we introduce the Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARSs) (Friedman, 1991), which is another machine learning algorithm with the ability to deal with spatial data. MARS is a simple and powerful nonparametric regression algorithm based on a divide et impera ("divide and conquer") strategy, partitioning the data sets into separate subsamples, with each region having its own regression line. This algorithm has two main objectives.

The first is to automatically select relevant variables in a classic regression model. The second allows the potential data non-linearities to be captured using a set of specific functions named base functions.

The MARS algorithm offers several advantages over other regression analysis methods. One of its main benefits is its ability to handle both numerical and categorical variables without the need for data preprocessing or hypotheses about data distribution. MARS also provides accurate results even when dealing with non-linear and high-dimensional data, which makes it ideal for complex problems. MARS generates models that are easy to interpret, creating a set of rules that can be easily understood and explained, making it an attractive option for any data analyst or scientist. In a way, MARS can be seen as an extension of the classic stepwise regression method based on the F statistic, where only significant independent variables are selected for the model. While stepwise regression introduces or drops variables linearly, the MARS algorithm selects only those pieces (base functions) of variables that may be relevant, combining them into a global model. Therefore, MARS is more flexible than stepwise regression and can capture non-linear relationships between predictor variables and the response variable.

In our view, MARS has two advantages over the most popular GAM. The first is its easy interpretation because it is based on linear basis function terms. Note that it is difficult to interpret GAM output. The second is that MARS drops the basic functions (BFs) that do not impact the model (similar to the F criteria in the classical backward/forward regression) and therefore improves the predictive ability. GAM includes all the variables, and part of this information may not be relevant (see Leathwick et al. (2006) for a comparison of both algorithms).
The MARS algorithm has been little used in regional science, even though it is frequently used in other fields.

For example, in finance, De Andrés et al. (2011) use MARS to forecast bankruptcy; Lee et al. (2006) apply it to mine customer credit; and Chattopadhyay and Mitra (2019) employ it to determine the price to be charged to customers for hotel rooms. In geography, Haleem et al. (2010) apply MARS to predict motor vehicle crashes, and in engineering, Zhang et al. (2015) utilize it in geotechnical earthquake engineering to analyze soil liquefaction. These are only some examples showing the multidisciplinary nature and popularity of the MARS methodology.

In this study, we focus on spatial econometrics for cross-sectional data (Anselin, 1988). The two objectives-the automatic selection of variables and non-linearities-have received unequal treatment in this field. With respect to the automatic selection of terms in spatial regression models, there were no specific methodologies developed to select the correct variable set, although some examples can be found (for example, Lan & Zhang, 2011 use stepwise selection terms in a spatial lag model). Further efforts were made to select the correct spatial term to incorporate into the spatial structure (Florax et al., 2003or Mur & Angulo, 2009), with procedures based on the use of several Lagrange Multiplier tests. In contrast, there is more literature accounting for non-linearities in spatial regression models (Basile et al., 2014;Eilers et al., 2015;Sangalli et al., 2013). Efforts to introduce non-linear models were mainly carried out in two ways. The first method includes specifications for limited dependent variables (for example, spatial tobit Xu & Lee, 2019, spatial probit models Martinetti & Geniaux, 2017, or spatial models to share data Xu & Lee, 2015. In the second method, several specifications emerged capturing non-linearities and avoiding functional form bias in models with Gaussian dependent variables. For example, Sangalli et al., 2013 consider Spatial Auto-regressive Semiparametric Geoadditive Models that combine penalized regression spline methods Eilers et al., 2015 with standard spatial autoregressive models. With a similar objective, Basile et al., 2014 combine penalized regression spline methods with standard cross-section spatial autoregressive models, developing a new typology of spatial regression models that includes spatial autoregressive terms within the same specification to capture spatial interaction and smooth terms to identify non-linear relationships between the response variable and the covariates (and the smooth function of the spatial coordinates and interaction between terms).

Moreover, there are numerous applied papers that include splines in spatial regression models with the aim of capturing non-linear effects. Good examples are Anselin and Le Gallo (2006) and Chasco et al. (2018), who include splines to model the impact of independent terms on the price of houses, or Brunauer et al. (2010), who apply additive mixed regression models to estimate hedonic price equations for rents in Vienna. Von Graevenitz and Panduro (2015) present an alternative to the standard spatial econometric model by modeling the spatial dimension of the housing market as a spatial GAM. Moreover, Basile (2009) uses a spatial non-linear Solow model to identify the pattern of labor productivity in Western Europe.

Despite its power, the MARS algorithm is seldom used in spatial econometrics. To the best of our knowledge, there are only a few regional economic studies using MARS: Martinetti and Geniaux (2017), De la Llave et al.

(2019a), Steurer and Hill (2020), and Yilmaz (2019). However, in the first step, all of them apply the MARS algorithm to make an automatic pre-selection of non-spatial covariates and, in the second step, they include the spatial term linearly.

This study fills this gap in the literature by showing how the MARS algorithm can work well in the framework of spatial regression models. By using MARS together with the instrumental variables (IV) (Kelejian & Prucha, 1998) estimation method, it is possible to identify the non-linear form of the terms in a spatial regression model, including the non-linear form of the spatial lag of the dependent variable using an unsupervised algorithm. Combining IV and the MARS algorithm in spatial regression models facilitates a computationally efficient estimation of complex relationships in spatial data. Both algorithms are computationally fast, enabling quick estimations of complex spatial models for big data sets. We present an example of MARS applications using a large data set with spatial autocorrelation: the flats for sale offered in St. Petersburg (Russia). We select the real estate market because it is typically characterized by non-linearity and spatial autocorrelation (Anselin & Le Gallo, 2006).

Therefore, the objective of this article is to show how a machine learning algorithm developed several decades ago can be a useful instrument to incorporate non-linear structures in spatial regression models. This novel method takes into account the natural non-linearity of the spatial effects in the classical spatial regression model. In short, our goal is simple: to put MARS into space.

The study is organized as follows. A short description of the MARS algorithm is presented in Section 2. Section 3 contains an empirical application of a spatial regression hedonic model using large data sets of dwellings in St. Petersburg. Section 4 shows empirical evidence of the non-linearity of the Wy term. Finally, the main conclusions appear in Section 5. Friedman (1991). This datadriven technique is particularly useful for identifying non-linearities in regression models without making previous assumptions about their functional form, explanatory variables, or number. The main characteristic of this methodology is that the econometric model considers different regression slopes in distinct intervals for each predictor. Unlike better-known linear regression techniques, MARS does not assume that coefficients are stable across the entire range of each variable and instead uses splines to fit piecewise continuous functions to model responses. In general, MARS constructs a piecewise linear function to capture non-linear relationships in an adaptive manner (Hoang et al., 2017). The principal advantage of this methodology, compared to similar algorithms (e.g., polynomial models or the GAM), is the simplicity of the resulting econometric model and its intuitive interpretation. Moreover, MARS models are reported to work satisfactorily in terms of computational cost, regardless of the dimension of the data set (Hastie et al., 2009), highlighting this algorithm's computational scalability for large sample sizes compared to other algorithms (see Table 10.1, p. 351).

div.head: MARS is a flexible, non-parametric, and piecewise regression technique introduced by
| The MARS algorithm
div.p: As with any regression model, the objective of this methodology is to build an econometric model to explain the variation of a dependent variable Y ¼ ðy 1 , …, y n Þ 0 with a set of potential explanatory variables X ¼ ðX 1 , …, X p Þ, where
div.formula: X i ¼ ðx 1i ,x 2i , …, x ni Þ 0 .
div.p: To achieve this classic objective, MARS uses the so-called BFs of the form ðx À cÞ þ ¼ maxf0, x À cg and ðc À xÞ þ ¼ maxf0,c À xg, where the subscript "+' ' means that the function takes only the positive value or zero in the case of a negative difference.
Formally, BF is expressed as:
div.formula: ðX i À cÞ þ ¼ maxf0, X i À cg ¼ X i À c, ifX i > c 0, otherwiseð1Þ
ðc À X i Þ þ ¼ maxf0, c À X i g ¼ c À X i , ifX i < c 0, otherwiseð2Þ
div.p: Such pairs of linear functions are called hinge functions (or two-sided truncated functions), and the constant c denotes a knot where the slope changes. The collection of all possible BFs, C,
div.formula: C ¼ fðx À cÞ þ ,ðc À xÞ þ g with c fx 1i , x 2i , …,x ni g andi ¼ 1,…, pð3Þ
div.p: is used to construct the econometric model. Each function is piecewise linear with a knot c at every x ij , and if all the input values are distinct, there are np hinge functions or equivalently 2np BFs. Using these BFs, the model-building strategy is similar to a classic forward stepwise regression, which uses the functions from the set C and their products as inputs. The final expression of the model is as follows:
div.formula: Y ¼ β 0 þ X M m¼1 β m h m ðXÞ þ ϵ,ð4Þ
div.p: where h m ðXÞ is a BF or a product of two or more such functions if interactions between variables are permitted, or perhaps the original predictor if it has a linear impact on the dependent variable. The coefficients β m are estimated by minimizing the sum of the squared (residual) errors (SSE), similar to a standard linear regression model.

div.head: | The forward pass
div.p: The model-training process iteratively selects and adds some hinge functions to the model (or the original predictor).

During each step of the training process, MARS selects new terms that minimize the SSE using ordinary least squares (OLS). In this forward pass, the MARS algorithm starts with a single model including only the intercept term β 0 . At each subsequent step, a reflected pair of hinge functions and an original predictor are selected and added to the model. The selected pair of hinge functions and original predictor can enter the model directly. Alternatively, they can be multiplied by an existing BF that is already in the model, thus becoming new BFs. The second case allows the modeling of the interaction between and/or among different predictors. The forward pass continues until it meets one of many conditions, such as: (i) the maximum number of model terms (chosen by the user) before pruning is reached; or (ii) when adding a term changes R 2 to less than a threshold value selected by the user (e.g., 0.001). The search for hinge functions at each step can be carried out using brute force, but this search can be sped up with a heuristic that reduces the number of parent terms to consider (Friedman, 1993).

In general, at the end of this process, we have a large model in the form described by equation ( 3). The MARS model obtained in this forward pass is adaptive and can exhibit a great degree of flexibility that can ultimately result in overfitting if no measures are taken to counteract it. To solve the overfitting problem and build a model with better generalization ability, a pruning procedure must be applied.

div.head: | The pruning process
div.p: Although there are other methods, MARS typically applies a backward deletion procedure to prune the model. Thus, in the second phase of the MARS algorithm, a "one-at-a-time" backward deletion procedure is applied during which the basis function with the least contribution to the model is repeatedly eliminated. This pruning is based on the generalized cross-validation (GCV) criterion originally proposed by Craven and Wahba (1979) and adapted by Friedman and Silverman (1989). The expression of GCV is:
div.formula: GCV ¼ 1 n P n i¼1 ðy i À b y i Þ 2 1 À ĈðMÞ n h i 2 ,ð5Þ
div.p: where ŷi are the fitted values and ĈðMÞ ¼ CðMÞ þ dK and CðMÞ is the number of parameters being estimated (the number of linearly independent basis functions without the intercept term); K is the number of knots selected in the forward process, and d represents the cost for each BF optimization. Usually, d ¼ 2 if the model does not involve interaction terms, and d ¼ 3 otherwise (Friedman, 1991). Thus, the GCV formula adjusts the SSE to take the flexibility of the model into account. Larger values of d result in fewer knots and smoother function estimates. The best MARS approximation is the one with the lowest GCV value. To get a measure similar to R 2 , the GCV coefficient can be standardized, and a new coefficient is defined as:
where GCV.tot is the GCV of a model with only the intercept term.

Note that the raw SSE is inadequate for comparing models because the SSE always increases as MARS terms are dropped, and, hence, the application of this criterion in the backward pass always results in selecting the largest model. Therefore, the GCV criterion is used to find the overall best model from a sequence of fitted models. The backward pass starts with the full model returned by the forward pass. Then, at each step, it deletes the term that results in the submodel with the lowest SSE. This iterative process continues until reaching the model with only the intercept. The backward pass then selects the final model: the submodel with the lowest GCV.

div.head: | Hyperparameter tuning the MARS algorithm
div.p: The model's parameters must be tuned to avoid overfitting in the machine learning application. There are several tuning parameters associated with the MARS algorithm that researchers can select: the threshold to determine when forward stepping should terminate; the minimum number of observations between nodes; the choice of variables to be included in linear form; the order of interaction between variables; and the maximum or minimum number of nodes. This list is not exhaustive, and more information is available, for example, in Kuhn et al. (2013).

div.head: | Non-linearity of the Wy term in the spatial econometric context

This is a relevant question in spatial econometrics, and several authors (Kelejian & Piras, 2014;Qu & Lee, 2015) include endogenous W matrices where spatial weights are determined by economic factors. For example, Kelejian and Piras (2014) try to find IVs for endogenous weights by regressing these spatial weights on exogenous variables, while Qu and Lee (2015) provide three estimation methods. Of course, higher-order spatial lag models could be estimated using these algorithms, but the MARS algorithm has the advantage of proving the cut points.

div.head: | THE MARS ALGORITHM: ST. PERTERSBURG HOUSING MARKET
div.p: This section illustrates the application of the MARS algorithm for the estimation of a hedonic model of housing prices in St. Petersburg and evaluates the sensitivity of this algorithm to the automatic selection of non-linear terms. We develop a hedonic model of the asking prices for dwellings in condominiums in St. Petersburg, which is the secondlargest city in Russia. We consider dwellings offered for sale in multi-family buildings, since these represent the bulk of St. Petersburg's housing stock. According to the results of the All-Russia 2010 census, in St. Petersburg only 18,584 households out of 1,882,236 lived in single-family houses, which make up less than 1%. 2The data are collected from the website EMLS (https://emls.ru/) and comprise over 17,000 announcements published in 2017 (N ¼ 16,959). They contain some basic information about the structural characteristics of dwellings and the buildings in which they are located. Additional locational features are derived using the coordinates of dwellings and various urban amenities, such as city center, subway stations, restaurants, and schools, (see Kholodilin et al., 2020). Table 1 contains the definitions of the variables and the main descriptive statistics. Figure 1 shows the spatial distribution of advertised dwellings in St. Petersburg. The distribution of dwellings corresponds to the built-up areas of the city. Figure 2 shows the flowchart presenting the overview of the modeling scheme followed in this section.
The objective of estimating 10 different models is to show how the MARS algorithm works with different restrictions.

For the sensitivity exercise, we select four tuning parameters: linpreds to force a variable to be included linearly into the model; thresh, which is the threshold in the increase of R 2 in the forward pass; endspan and minspan to control the minimum number of observations between knots (minspan) and before the first and after the final knot (endspan). Other tuning parameters can be selected as well: for example, degree of interaction or the maximum number of terms before the pruning pass.

Table 2 shows the estimation results for five models, SP-1 through SP-5, with different tuning parameters. The models are estimated in two steps. Step 1: The MARS algorithm is used to select the relevant variables or BFs using the tuning parameters shown in the first rows of Table 2. In this step, all the variables listed in Table 1 are included in the MARS algorithm.

Step 2: A classical Spatial Lag Model is estimated by IV (Kelejian & Prucha, 1998), using the usual instruments for the spatially lagged dependent variable: the BFs obtained in step 1 as well as the first and second spatial lags of those BFs.

The definition of the spatial weights matrix, W=ðw ij Þ, is based on a combination of two criteria. First, w ij ¼ 1 if the distance between the observations i and j is less than 100 m, and 0 otherwise. Second, if an observation does not have neighbors using this criterion (a total of 1346 observations do not have neighbors using this criteria), the two-nearest neighbor criterion is used to connect this observation. Due to the uneven distribution of dwellings, by selecting a short distance (e.g., 60 m), a large number of dwellings are isolated (2631 dwellings). On the contrary, if we consider a longer distance (e.g., 140 m), many dwellings will have too many neighboring houses (more than 600 neighbors). The results for a distance of 80 m; 120 m; 10-nearest neighbors, and 20-nearest neighbors are shown in Annex B (Table B1) to assess the robustness of the results with respect to the definition of the W matrix. Model SP-1 is the baseline model, and all the variables are forced to be included linearly in the MARS algorithm.
This is the case of a classical SLM model. All the variables are statistically significant and have the expected signs.

The three dummy variables have positive signs, showing that the price increases if elevators and balconies are available and the dwelling is in good condition. The two variables for distance have negative signs, showing that when the distance increases, the price decreases. The number of restaurants and schools in the neighborhood has a positive sign showing that more services around dwellings increase the price. Finally, the coefficient of spatial dependence takes the value of 0.226 and is statistically significant.

Models SP-2 through SP-5 are spatial models, and the 11 variables listed in Table 1 are supplied as inputs to the MARS algorithm. Note that the MARS algorithm can consider whether to include each variable or not. If a variable is included, it can be included linearly or the algorithm can split it into several BFs and include all or some of them in the final model. Models SP-2 through SP-5 are estimated by IV.

Model SP-2 does not include the restriction of linearity of the X terms. After the forward/backward pass, the MARS algorithm selected only three variables in the final model: Surf, Room, and Dcenter, splitting the variables into six BFs. The remaining variables are found not to be relevant. The variable Surf is split into two BFs to consider different effects for dwellings with floor areas of less/more than 82.60 m 2 . The coefficient for the term ðSurf À 82:6Þ þ is 0.012 and, therefore, for each increase of 1 m 2 , the price increases by approximately 1.2% if the surface of the dwelling is greater than 82.6 m 2 . If the dwelling has less than 82.6 m 2 , the expected increase for each m 2 is 2.0% because the term ð82:6 À SurfÞ þ is À0.020. Similar results are obtained for Rooms and Dcenter, splitting both variables into two BFs; 4 is the knot for the number of rooms and 6.54 km is the knot for the distance from the city center. The number of terms selected by the algorithm in model SP-2 is low, mainly due to the selection of the value 0.01 for the thresh tuning parameter. The forward pass stops quickly when the increase of R 2 is lower than thresh ¼ 0:01 and, hence, the algorithm cannot go deep enough. Finally, the coefficient of spatial dependence is 0.184, lower than in SP-1.

In this case, MARS selects seven Surf variables, splitting them into 13 BFs. The number of variables and BFs is higher than in SP-2 because the forward pass stops when the increase of R 2 is lower than 0.001. Major changes emerge in SP-3. The dummy variable GoodCond is included, and several structural characteristics (Floor and NFloor) and locational characteristics (Dsubway) are relevant. The MARS algorithm includes several BFs of these variables. The spatial term Wy is statistically significant with a similar value to that obtained in the model SP-2.

Two considerations should be kept in mind with respect to model SP-3. First, the variable Rooms is split into three BFs with two knots: 2 and 4. In the sample, only 252 dwellings have more than four rooms as these types of dwellings are not typical in Russia. Knot 4 is very close to the maximum value of the variable (see Table 1). Second, the variable Dcenter is split into three BFs with the knots at 1.11 and 6.54 km. An inspection of the sample identifies only 43 houses with distances shorter than 1.11 km from the center of St. Petersburg. In both cases, the MARS selection of BFs can lead to overfitting. This problem can be solved by tuning the algorithm to control the minimum number of observations between consecutive knots and after the final knot (or before the first knot). Alternatively, we can tune the algorithm to specify the maximum number of knots per predictor. With the objective of reducing the risk of overfitting, we change the tuning parameters for the next two models.

Model SP-4 is obtained by selecting thresh ¼ 0:001 and at least 1500 observations between contiguous knots and before (after) the first (last) knot. This new set of tuning parameters leads to some changes in the output of

Models SP-1 through SP-5 forced the spatial term Wy to be included linearly, as is usual in spatial econometrics. We relax this restriction using the MARS algorithm: It is possible that the change in prices of the nearest dwellings has a varied impact on the price of a particular dwelling depending on the value of those nearby dwellings. To test whether this hypothesis holds for St. Petersburg, we drop the linearity restriction for the term Wy, when the MARS algorithm is applied.

div.head: | Non-linear spatial term Wy
div.p: In this subsection, we estimate five models using the MARS algorithm with the same tuning parameters that are used in Section 3. The results from applying this estimation procedure are shown in Table 3.

The hypothesis that we propose in this paper is that the price of houses does not depend linearly on the price of surrounding homes. There is a non-linear relationship. Identifying the specific type of non-linearity may vary depending on the housing market being studied. The MARS algorithm is used in this subsection to identify nonlinearities based on a data-driven exercise for the specific housing market of St. Petersburg.

In the model SP-MARS-1, the tuning parameters force all the X variables (if they are relevant for the MARS algorithm) to be included linearly, with the exception of Wy, which can be split into several BFs. Thanks to MARS, the level of spatial dependence is allowed to depend on the value of the neighboring dwellings. If a house is surrounded by dwellings with values lower than 8.89 (7260 rubles), the coefficient of spatial dependence is 0.278. However, if the dwelling is surrounded by houses with a mean value higher than 8.89, this coefficient is 0.184 and, therefore, the impact on the price is lower.

Models SP-MARS-2 through SP-MARS-4 allow non-linearity in the X variables. No relevant changes are observed compared to models SP-2 through SP-4; the selection of variables and knots is similar. With respect to the non-linearity of the Wy term, in all the models the MARS algorithm considers it relevant to split this term into several BFs. Like in Section 3.1, a CV exercise was carried out to find the optimal hyperparameters (Figure 6). The results obtained are very similar to those obtained when the term Wy is included linearly. Therefore, the same hyperparameters are selected to reduce the overfitting (Thresh ¼ 0:001; minspan ¼ 8000; Endspan ¼ 0). The last column of Table 3 shows the result of the estimation of this model. The SP-MARS-5 model splits the term Wy into two BFs.

Figure 7 shows the slopes of the two BFs. If the dwellings have a logarithm of price lower than 8.59 (5378 rubles), the coefficient of spatial dependence has a negative impact of À0.059 (see the definition of the term ðc À WyÞ þ ).

Value 8.59 is the 49 percentile ( < P 49 ) of the dwelling's price (in log), and therefore, there is a negative impact on the price if a dwelling has houses around it with lower prices ( < P 49 ). For dwellings with prices above 5378 rubles, the impact of the neighboring dwellings is positive 0.237. Therefore, there is a positive impact if there are houses with higher prices ( > P 49 ) around it. The results obtained with this methodology can be compared to GAM's, in Annex A.

To conclude this Section, we must highlight that the non-linear impact of the Wy term on the y variable, in the case of the housing market, is a more realistic hypothesis than the classical linear impact in hedonic models. However, the emergence of big data has brought new challenges to spatial econometrics, as the classic techniques used in the past may no longer be adequate for large data sets (Arbia et al., 2019). One of the challenges of dealing with big data sets is the issue of maximum likelihood estimation. Maximum likelihood estimation is a popular method for estimating model parameters, but it can be computationally expensive and time-consuming when dealing with large data sets. When the data set is large, this calculation can become very complex and computationally intensive.

To overcome this challenge, alternative algorithms to the classical maximum likelihood estimation method are needed. The MARS algorithm (Friedman, 1991) could be an effective solution. The MARS algorithm is a nonparametric regression technique that can be used to model complex relationships between variables. It can handle large data sets efficiently, and it automatically selects the optimal model structure. The MARS algorithm can also produce simple and easy-to-interpret models, estimate the contributions of input variables, and is computationally efficient. Another challenge that arises when working with big data sets is the assumption of linearity in the relationship between variables. In many cases, the assumption of linearity may not hold, and non-linear relationships between variables may exist. The MARS algorithm is well suited to address this challenge, as it can include non-linear terms in the model, which is not possible with classical linear regression models.

In spatial econometrics, including the spatial lag of the dependent variable in a non-linear way is an essential issue to be addressed. The Wy term is typically included linearly in spatial lag models, but it is reasonable to think that this term, like the WX terms, can have a non-linear impact on the spatial regression model (Debarsy & Verardi, 2010). By using the MARS algorithm to include the spatial lag of the dependent variable in a non-linear way, we can gain valuable insights into the relationship between variables in spatial econometrics. This approach can provide more accurate estimates and better predictions compared to classical linear regression models. In the specific case of hedonic models, it is natural to think that the impact of the price of houses in a neighborhood depends on the value of neighboring houses, and, therefore, non-linear effects must be included in this variable (Zou et al., 2022). This fact is relevant for the spatial econometrics literature, and more research is needed to account for the natural non-linear effects of spatial dependence in spatial lag models.

In conclusion, the MARS algorithm, in conjunction with the IV method (Kelejian & Prucha, 1998), can offer an effective solution for handling big data sets and including non-linear terms. By including the spatial lag of the dependent variable in a non-linear way, we can gain valuable insights into the relationship between variables in spatial econometrics. This can help us to better understand the underlying processes that drive spatial phenomena and provide more accurate predictions for future outcomes.

There are alternative approaches to the MARS algorithm that allow spatial heterogeneity in spatial econometric models, such as the mixture model (Cornwall & Parent, 2017), quantile regression (Seya et al., 2020), functionalcoefficient models (Koroglu & Sun, 2016), the penalized spline combined with spatial error model (Łaszkiewicz et al., 2022), and SAR-(M)GWR (Geniaux & Martinetti, 2018). Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses, and the choice of method will depend on the specific research question and the characteristics of the data.
Researchers should carefully consider the assumptions and limitations of each approach and choose the method that best suits their research objectives.

Resumen. Multivariate Adaptive Regression Spline (MARS) es un algoritmo de aprendizaje automático no paramétrico sencillo y potente que automatiza la selección de términos no lineales en modelos de regresión. En este estudio se propone utilizar MARS en un marco de regresión espacial para tener en cuenta las posibles no linealidades y los efectos espaciales en los modelos de regresión espacial. Se examinó el funcionamiento de este algoritmo utilizando un conjunto de datos relativamente grande de 17.000 viviendas en San Petersburgo (Rusia). Las pruebas empíricas muestran que la mayoría de las variables explicativas del modelo de regresión espacial, incluido el desfase espacial de la variable dependiente, tienen un impacto no lineal en los precios de venta de las viviendas.

div.head: | Hyperparameter search
div.p: Like other machine learning algorithms, the MARS output depends on several tuning parameters (Section 2.4). A cross-validation (CV) exercise can be done to identify the optimal combination of these hyperparameters. In this paper, the objective of our CV exercise is to carry out a parameter grid search to improve the predictive power of the model and therefore reduce probable overfitting. Basically, a training subsample (in-sample) is selected, and the MARS algorithm is applied. The model obtained is applied to predict the housing values in the test subsample (outof-sample). This procedure is repeated T times, randomly selecting training and test subsamples. The MRSE in the out-of-sample is obtained in each iteration, and the mean value of the MRSE is used as an indicator of overfitting.

Developing a CV exercise in a spatial framework presents some problems (Brenning, 2012;Deppner & Cajias, 2022;De la Llave et al., 2019b;Karasiak et al., 2022). Note that a critical requirement for a CV exercise is that the training and test subsamples must be independent. In a spatial context, all observations are related to each other, and therefore, the in-and out-of-samples are not independent. To minimize this problem, we apply the k-means algorithm to spatial coordinates to create k ¼ 9 spatially compact and non-overlapping subsamples (as proposed by Deppner & Cajias, 2022and Brenning, 2012). Then, (k À 1) folds are used for training the model, and the kth fold is used for testing. Since the k-means algorithm generally gives different results each time it is executed, to obtain a robust selection of hyperparameters, the process is repeated 200 times (T ¼ 200), and the mean of the RMSE is obtained. Figure 4 shows two maps with examples of how to split the data into k-folds.

The hyperparameters select to make the grid search are 3 : 1. Minspan ¼ 11,500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000 2. Endspan ¼ 0, 500 3. Thresh ¼ 0:05, 0.01, 0.005, 0.001, 0.0005 4. MaxKnots ¼ 1, 2, 3, 4 For every combination of these parameters, the MARS algorithm is executed using the training sample, and the resulting model is then utilized to make predictions on the test sample. The RMSE is then calculated to evaluate the accuracy of the predictions. A total of 110 MARS models have been launched T ¼ 200 times each. Figure 5 (left) shows the mean values of the mean of the RMSE of the prediction out-of-sample. 4 The minimum value of RMSE is obtained for Thresh ¼ 0:001 and Minspan ¼ 8000 (RMSE mean ¼ 0:2073). This result confirms that for prediction proposes, a simple model with a reduced number of knots is preferred. Figure 5 (right) shows in several violin plots the estimated ρ values for Thresh ¼ 0:001 and different values of Minspan and MaxKnots. For all the in-sample models, the spatial autocorrelation is significant, with ρ values around 0.2. Model SP-5 shows the output of the MARS algorithm with the select hyperparameters. Some changes occur compared to model SP-4. There are different knots because the algorithm forces the selection of evenly spaced knots for each predictor. 3 No interaction between variables is considered. Interaction at a lower degree can help interpret the final model, whereas higher-order interactions can cause inconsistencies in model predictions on rare occasions (Naser et al., 2022). 4 Only results for Endspan ¼ 0.
